newsitem.title: JAPAN: Thai rescue package may provide future blueprint.
newsitem.headline: Thai rescue package may provide future blueprint.

text.p: An international aid package aimed at bailing out Thailand is likely to be a blueprint for coping with future regional financial crises, though markets have yet to be convinced the Thai rescue itself will succeed.

Senior finance officials from the Asia-Pacific region on Monday hammered out the rescue package, pledging a total of $16 billion in loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Asian nations led by Japan.

The loan package -- the largest to a single country since the IMF and donors led by the United States made nearly $40 billion available to Mexico in 1995 -- included $4 billion each from the IMF and Japan.

Australia, Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong each kicked in $1 billion while South Korea and Indonesia will each lend $500 million. Another $3 billion is expected to come from the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and possibly China.

"When you look at the package...it's multilateral, evenly spread, it's a very broad-based consensus and as a result should...another country be in need, it could easily be replicated," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan.
Asian contributions to the package ended up larger than expected. Japan's contribution, still by far the largest for a single nation, was smaller than initially anticipated.
The United States, meanwhile, welcomed the Thai package but will not be contributing any of its own funds.

"I think certain precedents were set in terms of elements such as Asia solidarity," said one diplomat familiar with the talks. "Certainly, there had been a reticence in the past for various countries to get together," the diplomat added, noting South Korea in particular had tended to shy away from regional cooperative efforts.

Behind the regional show of solidarity was clearly a fear that a failed Thai rescue effort would boost chances that other countries whose economies face problems and whose currencies have also come under attack would also end up in need of help.

Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam said Hong Kong's participation was prompted by what it saw as a need to support Asian monetary cooperation and to counter currency turmoil in the region.
"(It) was very, very important because there was always the danger of a contagion effect affecting economies in this region," Yam told Reuters Financial Television on Monday.
Australia, meanwhile, doubtless had political as well as economic motives for its decision to contribute more than many had expected.
"Australia is trying to prove its point that it is a legitimate member of various Asian circles and that when push comes to shove...they pay their dues," the diplomat said.

More broadly, the rescue plan was the culmination of lengthy discussions in a variety of venue among Asia-Pacific economies which feared that the region would ultimately face its own version of the Mexican peso crisis.

"Everyone had thought that there was this sort of systemic risk in Asia and that they needed to create ways to cope," said one Japanese economist. "Now, if a similar problem occurs, they will be able to cope adequately."

Japanese Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara, a vocal proponent of deeper Asian cooperation in financial and monetary matters, said on Monday the concerted action by the Asia-Pacific nations showed their "firm resolve to cope with such problems in the future."
"We would like to deepen cooperation in many ways but as for a permanent institution to deal with such problems, there is no specific plan at the moment," Sakakibara added.
Future regional rescues, should they be needed, would likely again rely on the IMF to set conditions for the troubled country's economic reform programme, analysts said.
At the same time, Japan is all but certain to ante up a hefty chunk of any required funds.

Tokyo, once reluctant to take a more active role on the Asian monetary front, has altered that wary stance and is now willing to assume a regional role similar to that of the United States in the Latin American region.
"Japan is always going to be a major contributor (in Asia) just as Germany would be to an east European bailout and the United States to a Latin American bailout," Koll said.
